speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
When this resolution was presented by my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Good)

Tax Collections

For these reasons I shall have to oppose the resolution.
Mr. HANCE J. LOGAN (Cumberland): I may say that after the reference made a few days ago bv the Acting Minister of Finance I brought	this	matter up	in	the PublicAccounts committee, of which I am chairman, and asked	them	for their	instructions. Amotion was made to request this House to give the committee power to make the inquiry as desired	by the hon.	member forBrant (Mr. Good). The motion was duly put to a vote and defeated, largely on the ground that it -was considered too late in the session to	enter	upon such	a	very serious
consideration, and secondly that there was a question as to whether the Public Accounts committee should not be confined to examining the public accounts and not determining what is public policy.

I took it that this would be the attitude of the government. Under the circumstances, therefore, I feel under an obligation to put myself on record briefly in regard to the need for this motion. I should like, in the first place, to refer to some of the significant and salient facts brought out during the investigation. In the first place the commissioner was formerly the tariff officer of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and was subsequently called upon as Commissioner of Taxation to assess the business profits and income taxes against concerns for whom he had previously been a special agent. In the second place the commissioner assumed full and personal responsibility for all appointments made under the Business Profits War Tax Act, and also for all adjustments or modifications of assessment made under that act. In the third place, among approximately
30.000	taxpayers assessed under the Business Profits War Tax Act not a single appeal was pressed and no board of referees was ever appointed. There was not one among the
30.000	who -was not satisfied to such an extent that he did not press his appeal; not one was irreconcilable. In the fourth place no member of parliament, and no committee of parliament, has had the privilege of examining any original assessment or any subsequent modification thereof. All the files are strictly confidential, and all the officials are under a solemn obligation to preserve secrecy. Not only is this obligation imposed upon all officials under the Business Profits War Tax
Act and the Income War Tax Act, but in addition, within the last year, all the officials in the Taxation branch at Ottawa have been required! to make a sweeping and solemn declaration before the commissioner.

National officials are without authority to accept coal shipments to Ontario at reduced rates. It is a perplexing situation. speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Some difficulty appears to
have arisen with the coal shipments, but I am not clear as to what the difficulty is. Negotiations have been carried on between the Alber.a government and the coal company. We agreed to provide one dollar per ton for this trial shipment of 25,000 tons to be brought from a centrad point in Alberta to a central point in Ontario, provided, of course, that the rate to be fixed was $7 a ton. I was given to understand that was the rate. That was the rate agreed upon as the initial rate, the railways claiming it cost $9 a ton. Checkers were to be appointed by the railway and by the Alber.a government. I think Mr. Hinton was paid by the Alberta government as their representative, but a careful check of the movement was to be kept from an Alberta point to a central point in Ontario. If it developed that the cost was more than $7 this government was to contribute to the extent of $1 per ton, and if it developed that it cost more than SS per ton the Alberta government was to contribute to the extent of one dollar. That was the arrangement as I understand, and that is the arrangement we are prepared to carry out.

It can be readily seen that this state of affairs could not continue. Now, there are two things that parliament can do; it can insist on having the Crowsnest agreement remain in force in its entirety or it can remove it altogether from the statute books. But a third and middle course might be taken, and we are asking parliament to remove from the agreement that part relating to westbound traffic, leaving to the prairies and the west for the future all the benefit they have ever received, and more too, I think, on grain and flour.
Now, suppose we said that the best thing to do was to leave the Crowsnest pass agreement in its entirety. I do not think there is a man in this House who in private would, after considering the situation, say that that ought to be done. What does it mean? Speaking as Minister of Railways and adviser of the government on railway matters, I feel a serious responsibility for the condition of our railways at the present time. Not only are we responsible for the great Canadian Pacific Railway, but we are responsible for and proprietors of 22,600 miiles of our own railway; and while I am not pleading the cause of the railways, let us all keep in mind that this is the situation to which we cannot close our eyes and which we cannot ignore in discussing the question. As I said, I have a responsibility, but I want to be bold, I want to pass that responsibility, or the share that belongs to him or her, over to every member of this House, because I say without any hesitation that this parliament could break the railways of Canada if it so desired, and any action we take ought to be taken with at least full consideration. Now, what would happen if the Crowsnest pass agreement were maintained in its entirety? On a large list of commodities-

The railways of Canada-I say it advisedly-cannot stand that application.
Then take the other viewpoint: Should we abolish the Crowsnest pass agreement altogether? I may admit at once that there are a great many men in this House who believe that it is the proper thing to do.

Let me come to clause 4. I am more surprised than I could imagine about the objections to clause 4. Some people have construed clause 4 to mean that certain people might be shut out from going to the courts at any time under the Crowsnest pass agreement or its application. What clause 4 means and what it says is simply this, that it precludes a great deal of little, petty lawsuits that might be brought against the railways on account of the decision given.by the Board of Railway Commissioners as to rates under which certain tolls were collected, which the Supreme court says were wrong. The committee can readily understand that if some people paid fifty cents too much, there may be speculators in different parts of the Dominion who will buy up all these little claims and start sui's against the railways. All that clause 4 says and means is that the railways shall not be liable for action for filing and collecting tolls for a few months under the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and it cannot be construed into meaning anything else. Perhaps I have violated all the rules; but as I gave notice of these amendments a few days ago and put them on Hansard, I would not be discussing the principle of the bill in its entirety unless I included the discussion of the bill as it will be when amended. I put these proposed amendments on Hansard some days ago in order that hon. members might have them before them.
The order in council which has been printed and published covers quite a large territory, and it was the final answer to the application made against the ruling of the Board of Railway Commissioners, which finding in its entirety was postponed until after the judgment cf the Supreme court. What we need in Canada at the present time on this rate question is a compromise attitude by which we shall get rid of some of the complications and be able to get a more equitable adjustment of freight rates throughout the Dominion. I do not mean by that putting burdens on here and taking burdens' off there, but in the west and in the east a certain chaos exists that must be cleared up. Who shall clear it up? We believe the Board of Railway Commissioners has the power and is the best authority to clear that up. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) will note that in the order in council reference was made to the westbound traffic, and while this government feels and while I believe parliament will agree that the simplest and most effective way of clearing up the situation that now exists is to adhere, as is done in the bill to the Crowsnest pass agree-

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
ment as regards grain and flour, the Board
of Railway Commissioners, when it comes to carry out the instructions as contained in the order in council, will have to face this situation, that on the Pacific coast a new condition affecting the prairies has arisen. Last year approximately 50,000,000 bushels of grain went through Vancouver harbour, and a large proportion of the grain that, when the Crowsnest pass agreement went into force, was all intended to come east, is going west. When the board comes to decide the rates to be applied on grain in the prairie provinces, it will have to take into account the new conditions that exist now that did not exist some years ago. It will have to take into account the fact that we have really three transcontinental railways, one running into Prince Rupert and two running into Vancouver. It will have to take into account further the fact that a not inconsiderable portion of the prairies find it more convenient, easier, to ship their grain to the Pacific coast, and any Board of Railway Commissioners will certainly give full consider-a'ion to this new condition and see that the Pacific coast trade is treated properly in any decision handed down by that board.

speechtext:
The proposal to put the various sections of Canada in the position to feel that they are receiving reasonable and fair treatment in regard to the very important and complicated question of freight rates has been before parliament for some time. The matter has been before the country for a number of years, and at the opening of this session a few months ago the government informed parliament that they had addressed themselves to the whole situation and purposed introducing a measure which they expected and1 hoped would solve this all perplexing problem. Let us view the legislation which the minister (Mr. Graham) has now submitted to us. That this legislation solves the freight rates problem, or even that it offers a medium of compromise, I think no one will assert with any very great confidence. The measure before us now may answer, to the satisfaction of the government, a pledge to bring in legislation, but that it will relieve in the slightest degree the consciousness of unfair treatment now permeating certain sections of the country, I think cannot be claimed under any circumstances. Indeed, I believe it will accentuate that feeling.
It is not my intention to delay the committee with a long detailed analysis of this proposed legislation, but I want to make very clear my position in regard to it and to the
question of transportation in a broad way. I have argued in this House and before my own constituents and the people of my province for certain .principles which I think should underlie and govern the making of a freight rate structure. I have argued that the fixation of rates is. such a complicated problem that it should not be pitchforked into parliament, but rather that it should be dealt with by a competent board, that board in my estimation being the Board of Railway Commissioners. All through the years that this matter has been under discussion, indeed in recent years when it has been the most acute problem in my own province, I have adhered very closely to that stand. I believe that if the government had in its proposed legislation stuck strictly to that main principle there would not have been so much to complain of to-day; but they deviate from it in that they extract from a certain agreement, based upon a statute of 1897, one part and seek to perpetuate it in this bill.
Further, I took -the stand a year ago when this matter was before the Privy Council on appeal from the railway board, the stand that I have taken on the public platform, that the Crowsnest pass agreement had outlived its usefulness, that it was obsolete and should be abrogated. Among the reasons which I advanced then and repeat now why I think that course should be taken are the following. First, I contend that while the Crowsnest pass agreement was a contract between the Canadian Pacific Railway on the one hand and the people of Canada as represented by parliament and the government on the other band, if in the lifetime of the contract conditions so change that one or both of the parties consider that its terms should be varied to meet those conditions, such variation can be made with the consent of both contracting parties. Now as a matter of fact, the people of Canada at large and the government are convinced that that contract should be abrogated; and the Canadian Pacific Railway, the other party to the contract, has appealed to the railway board and the committee of the Privy Council for its abrogation. So I contend there is no obstacle to the setting aside of that contract.
Another reason why in my estimation the statute should be repealed is this. The contract was made in 1897 when the control of freight rates was far different from that which obtains to-day. At that time the railways filed their tariffs with the Department of Railways, and the Railway Committee of the Privy Council either approved or disapproved
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

them, as the ease might be. But in 1903 parliament, under the leadership of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, erected what is
5 p.m. known as the Board of Railway Commissioners. I pause here to repeat what I have said on other occasions, that of all the public acts of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that was the greatest of his career and one for which he and those who were associated with him deserve the fullest credit. That Board of Railway Commissioners won and held the confidence of the people of Canada for the way in which it administered this highly technical act, and only in the last couple of years has there been any question of the fairness of the board-with that I shall deal in a moment. With this change in conditions the usefulness of the Crowsnest pass agreement passed away; and I remind those who to-day seek to retain the agreement that down to 1916 the ordinary rates allowed by the Board of Railway Commissioners were not above those of the Crowsnest pass agreement, so there was no question of invoking the agreement to protect the public interest.

The war brought about a revolution in the economic structure of this and every other country. In other words, a dollar which previously would purchase a given quantity of goods, or in this case a certain quantity of freight service, shrunk so that it would not buy more than forty per cent and in some cases thirty per cent of what it did in prewar days-the purchasing power of the dollar was very much reduced. Therefore to-day under these new economic conditions it is not fair that there shall be a constant scale of freight rates. Transportation service must fluctuate in value the same as other services, or on the other hand ruin must come to those who are bound to carry on the transportation of the country.

But I have the opinion of those who are much better qualified to judge of the legal merits than I am, and I myself read that into the statute. My hon. friend knows it perfectly well. I do not wish to labour the point. As I have already stated twice, t'he minister by his amendment limits the application of clauses 6 and 5 to the territory previously covered by the Crowsnest pass agreement, and that did not apply to British Columbia.
I have before me a copy of the Vancouver Morning Sun of June 6, 1925, and on the front page I see the photographs of three lions of the Liberal party, Premier Oliver, the Hon. Dr. J. H. King, and Mr. G. G. McGeer. These are the three men to whom credit is due for what they secured for British Columbia at last, the opportunity of pleading its cause, as the Minister of Railways describes it, with a free hand. I wonder ryhat the Minister of Public Works has to say as to the amendment the Minister of Railways has introduced.
I wonder what the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay) has to say as to the amendment that the Minister of Railways has injected into this bill thus depriving him, depriving his province, and depriving his associates of the possibility of going before the railway board with free hands, literally tying their hands behind their backs. Let me read a passage or two from this eulogy of the minister :
It is only the first trench in the west's campaign for justice. To relax efforts now would be suicidal,
[Mr. Stevens.1
They look upon this order in council and this bill of the Minister of Railways as a great victory. The Sun has this further to say:
The Hon. J. H. King, British Columbia's representative in the Mackenzie King government, was radiant with optimism as he commented on the government's order that equalization of freight rates should be taken in hand forthwith.
What a travesty! What a mockery! Here the government come out with an order in council in which they say to the railway board in a sense: " Now go to work and equalize freight rates. Give to British Columbia, give to the Hon. Dr. King "-I am referring here to the Minister of Public Works- "give to the Hon. John Oliver, give to Mr. Jerry McGeer"-the $150,000 advocate of the provincial government-" the right to equalize freight rates," a thing they have been fighting for for years; and then having sent that broadcast over the country, having secured a considerable amount of acclamation from its people of that province, the Minister of Railways brings in this bill which deliberately hangs them after they have been eulogized in this fashion. The Sun goes on to say:
The railway board is to be unfettered in its investigation except in regard to the eastbound rates on grain and flour. On these the maximum established under the .Crownest pass Act is not to be exceeded.
On the interpretation of the order in council, on the interpretation of the bill as the Minister of Railways introduced it, the east-bound minimum rate was to apply to the westbound traffic as well; and the Minister of Public Works knows that. He knows that was expected. He knows that his friends in British Columbia congratulated him on obtaining that. Now the Minister of Railways interjects three little words-" in the territory "-and the whole dream, the whole aspiration, the entire hope is destroyed and proven to be only a delusion and a snare. It is not my intention to labour the point;
I simply want to make my own position clear. It is this: that insofar as the transportation problem is concerned I believe it should be left unfettered, and in the true sense unfettered, to the Board of Railway Commissioners.
I did intend to say a word regarding the Board of Railway Commissioners. I have heard some hon. members of this House say that they have not confidence in that board. The Hon. John Oliver, Premier of British Columbia, intimated in an interview which he gave the other day that he had not confidence in the Board of Railway Commissioners. I want to say that this circulating of the spirit of distrust in the Board of Railway Com-

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
missioners is one of the most lamentable things that I know of. I think it is unfortunate and wholly inexcusable. The Board of Railway Commissioners ought to have the confidence of the people of Canada, and if they are shackled by the government in going into this problem then they will have great difficulty in escaping the charge of being actuated by influences other than those of equity and justice. And so I say this government should be the last to interfere with the board in the free exercise of their powers and of their wisdom. I plead with this House that we should scrupulously avoid giving out to the public any idea that this court-one of the finest ever established in Canada-is anything but a sound, and a fair, and a just court. Having encouraged the confidence of the public in the Board of Railway Commissioners I believe our duty is to leave the problem with them free and unhampered from any restriction whatsoever.
I repeat again my other point and it is this: The Crowsnest pass agreement as sued is obsolete, it has outlived its usefulness. I agree with the minister that it is impossible, but I go further than the minister and say that a thing that is impossible, a thing that is obsolete, should be abrogated in toto, and not one section of it retained to pester and worry the people, and interefere with the harmonious and equitable adjustment of these matters.

speechtext:
I think we all realize the difficulty of the situation in regard to the railway problem in this Dominion of ours. Canada is a country of vast distances, with a sparse population and railway deficits to be met year after year. We want to keep these facts in mind at all times when discussing railway problems and railway rates. However, we recognize the fact that the railways must operate. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) in his speech this afternoon pictured a condition in which the railways would be unable to operate. Of course, we know that will never happen for the simple reason that the people of this country are interested in the railways and realize that their interests are indissolubly bound up with them. But there is another side to the situation. Agriculture and industry must also function, and we must endeavour to preserve, as far as we possibly can, a proper balance between the operation of our railways and the successful prosecution of agriculture and its allied industries, to say nothing of the industries of the country as a whole. These are things that we must keep in mind1.
I hope to convince the House that in speaking as I am I am not expressing any sectional point of view; that while I am speaking in behalf of certain interests and keeping them in mind, I am just as anxious as anyone else to see that the country as a whole shall prosper, that all parts of the Dominion shall get equal opportunities to prosper and progress as we hope they shall in the future. While dealing more particularly with the western prairie provinces anything that I may say will not be said in any sectional spirit, but due regard will be paid to the national interests os a whole.
The order-in-council which preceded the bill we are now discussing admits the principle of maximum rates. To prove the truth of that I shall read an extract from the order-in-council itself to the following effect:
The committee are further of the opinion that as the production and export of grain and flour forms one of the chief assets of the Dominion, and in order to encourage the further development of the great graingrowing provinces of the west, on which development the future of Canada in large measure depends, it is desirable that the maximum cost of the transportation of these products should be determined and known, and therefore are of opinion that the maximum established for rates on grain and flour, as at present in force under tfye Crowsnest pass agreement, should not be exceeded.
This is a frank admission that this question is not a local one but is a question of national importance which affects the prosperity of the whole Dominion. In dealing with the question of transportation and the different rates on grain from the west to the east comparisons are sometimes made between the rates on the Canadian side and the rates on the American side. In that connection I should like to read the following extract:
2.	The spring wheat areas of the northwestern states, Montana and the Dakotas, have the advantage of geographical location in being situated so much nearer lake Superior, and the great bulk of the grain is a comparatively short average haul as against the longer average haul from the prairie provinces to Fort William and Port Arthur.
3.	It had also, no doubt, in mind that the producers of the western provinces have to compete with the remainder of the world in marketing their wheat and the foremost competitor is the Argentina republic. The average haul from Argentina to the shipping ports is 140 miles. The average haul from the western provinces to lake Superior is between 800 and 900 miles and before the ocean haul begins there is the water haul, Fort William to Montreal, during the season of lake navigation, the average rate for which last year was about 11 cents per bushel.
4.	These rates on grain and flour from the prairie provinces to lake Superior were, with other rates on various commodities, provided for in the Crowsnest agreement between the government of Canada and the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1897. Several millions of dollars were paid the railway as a subsidy, as part of the bargain; the rates were thus bought and paid for.

The hon. member from

was given authority to disregard the Crowsnest pass agreement. In 1919, statutory authority was given to the railway commission to abrogate the agreement until July, 1922. In 1922, as most of us are aware, a special committee was appointed by this House to inquire into the whole matter of transportation costs. I happened to be a member of that committee, and I remember a good deal about the proceedings that took place at that time. I recall that President Beatty, President Hanna and other railway freight experts for the two different railways appeared before the committee and, I think, giving evidence upon oath, stated that if the Crowsnest pass rates came into effect on grain and flour, tremendous deficits would occur on their railways. If I remember correctly, President Beatty said that the loss on grain alone on the Canadian Pacific would be S14.000.000. and President Hanna said that the Canadian National Railways would lose $7,000,000. As a matter of fact, in the following year after the Crowsnest pass agreement had come into operation on those commodities the railways I think made more money than they had ever made before. Therefore, the lugubrious prophecies that these gentlemen made at that particular time were entirely wrong. They were many million dollars out. The final report on Crowsnest pass rates on grain and grain products was submitted to f his House. I am sorry to say that hon, members to my right opposed that report very strenuously and took exactly same stand as they take to-day. They do not move. They seem just to stay put all the time. Therefore, I am afraid we are not- going to get from them very much support along the lines that I would advocate this afternoon.

speechtext:
That condition of affairs remained until July 6 of last year when the Crowsnest pass agreement came again into full force. It is needless for me to take up any of the time of the committee in discussing what has happened since then. We know that immediately after it came into operation we had railway rate discrimination.
I am not very much concerned so far as that goes as to what happens to the bill that is before the House at the present time. I feel prefectly satisfied that in any case neither
[Mr. Forke.J
the government nor the railways could allow this matter of discrimination to continue. I have an idea that it was rather clever strategy on the part of the railways just to bring about the condition of affairs that now exists by putting that into effect, and I do not think that discrimination can or will continue, no matter what happens to the legislation that is now before the House. We>
had the decision of the railway commission that, instead of remedying the discrimination, wiped the agreement off the slate altogether. My hon. friends to the right say that we should have complete faith in the railway commission. That sort of thing did not tend to give us very _ great faith in at least some of their decisions. Then we had the decision of the Supreme court, and again we have the Crowsnest pass rates put into effect with the discrimination that has been spoken about this afternoon. Finally we now have the amendment which is before the House.
Why is the west anxious for statutory maximum rates? The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), in his very eloquent speech this afternoon, wonders why the west want any particular legislation in regard to railway rates. The western prairie provinces occupy a postion that cannot be parallelled anywhere else in the civilized world at the present time in regard to agricultural conditions. We have in those three western pro-vinees a great agricultural empire and yet we are in the centre of a continent far removed from the seaports where the products of those prairies must find an outlet. Consequently, they demand more serious attention than any other particular section of the country in regard to transportation costs. Transportation is vital to the prairie provinces. With rates that are unprofitable, rates that are too high to permit the carriage of agricultural products, it means bankruptcy for those provinces. Why are we anxious to have some maximum rates fixed? In the first place, it has been pointed out that the east has competition by lake and river to the sea, whereas in the west no such condition exists. British Columbia, which I am sure ' has many strong advocates in this House, enjoys ocean communication; it is a maritime province with seaports right at hand. British Columbia therefore is in many respects in a different position from the prairie provinces. The west wants maximum rates fixed, and fixed by an agreement, simply for the purpose of protecting itself from any exorbitant railway rates that it may be called upon to pay at any time. It is all very well to say, why not trust the railway commission? Well, certain things

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
have been promised us by solemn compact and we wish those things fulfilled; certain conditions exist which we want to see continue for our protection. For twenty-seven years we have had a certain agreement and now we are asked to give it up and trust to something else which we are told may prove as satisfactory. We are asked to trust to the railway commission, which would already have entirely wiped out this agreement if it had had the power to do so.
The commission is supposed to fix rates adequate to ensure reasonable dividends. Perhaps that is the first consideration with the railway commission-the fixing of rates to provide adequate dividends to the railways. But there is another point of view which one may take with regard to railway rates, that is, reasonable rates as between the railways and the communities served. That, I take it, should be the proper function of the railway commission. We feel a little uncertainty in giving up something sure which we already have for something else the nature of which we cannot conceive; and consequently I am inclined to stand solidly behind our agreement until we know exactly what we shall get. Maximum rates may occasion some trouble for the railways; but there is a great deal of trouble in this world anyway, and nobody gets a smooth path to travel all the way. . The present amendment to the Crowsnest rates is to apply to grain and flour, while the rest of commodities are to go by the board. And what do we get in return? I have them here, taken from Hansard, and I think they are correct. The railways were prepared at that time to make certain reductions in lieu of the Crowsnest pass agreement. There was to be a twenty per cent reduction on grain rates, two-thirds of the way to the Crow rates, when ten per cent would have brought it to the level of those rates. speechtext: The House resumed consideration in committee of Bill 181 to amend the Railway Act, 1919, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext:
Continuing the remarks I
made before six o'clock, I would like to say that in seeking the advantages we do under the Crowsnest pass agreement the west does not desire any favours at the expense of any other part of Canada. Nor are we animated in any way by a feeling of hostility to the railway companies. I think every one of us recognizes the fact that the railways and the people are inseparably bound together as far

Railway Freight Rates
as the prosperity of our country is-concerned. So that when we seek to have maximum rates fixed by statute it is not with any idea of being hostile to the railway companies. The west, if it should prosper and develop as it ought to do, will in a few years produce a vast amount of freight both outgoing and incoming. Rightly or wrongly we believe that the solution of our railway problems lies very largely in the development of western Canada. There is no hostility towards, and no desire on our part bo belittle, any other section or province in the Dominion, but we believe that in the west there is boundless room for expansion, room for a very large increase in population, with the result that the volume of freight both outgoing and incoming will be enormously increased. Consequently the prosperity of the west is indeed vital to this Dominion. Furthermore, it seems to me that this question of transportation rates is so vital that unless a proper solution is arrived at it will mean that the people out there will enjoy but a bare existence, or a degree of prosperity much less than they would under more favourable conditions. If the railways could show by any process of bookkeeping that the west was enjojdng a cheaper rate than is enjoyed in eastern Canada, I think we would be quite amenable to reason and would be willing that our rates should be raised. On the other hand, we conscientiously believe that the west is paying its full share of rates at the present time, and that no other part of Canada is being sacrificed at the expense of the prairie provinces through the Crowsnest pass rates being put into operation.

Does the hon. member
suggest that British Columbia has not been sacrificed by the Crowsnest pass agreement?

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919

I would not agree to that
proposition. At the same time I do not think we are showing any hostility to British Columbia or any other portion of Canada.

I was asking whether the hon. member thought that some injustice had not been done to British Columbia as a result of the Crowsnest pass agreement and the schedule of rates proposed in this bill.

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext:
I cannot enter into an argument on that point. But as I stated, we were quite willing that all freight from the western provinces should have the benefit of the Crowsnest pass agreement.
Another thing we must keep in mind, no matter what difficulties British Columbia may labour under, is that she is a maritime province, has ports on the seashore and derives benefits therefrom which we do not enjoy in the prairie provinces at the present time. We hope that the time is not far distant when we shall have a port to the north of us in the prairie provinces, which will help to reduce freights. I might also mention another fact in connection with the prairie provinces. They are not in the least selLcontained. They ship out and ship in. Westbound freight is very important to the prairie provinces for the simple reason that they are not manufacturing to any extent. Most of the goods they require are transported over a thousand miles, so that it is easily seen that westbound freight is very important to the prairie provinces. Perhaps the day is not as far distant as some of us might suppose when the prairie provinces will be to some extent more self-contained than they are at the present time, but it is vital to them that they should get the best rates possible both east and west, and it is perfectly natural, and only just and right, that when we have the agreement, something that has been bought and paid for, we should get the benefit of it, and we are loth to see a law placed upon the statutes of the Dominion that will abrogate any privileges we have enjoyed during the past twenty-seven years.
A good many people in our Dominion, I am afraid, wrongly conclude that they have to pay for the concessions which have been granted under the Crowsnest pass agreement. I do not admit for one moment that the west has not all the time been paying for the privileges which it enjoyed by having railway communication. That there have been deficits on the railway we all know, and we are all anxious that these deficits should be wiped out just as soon as possible, but I can see no future for our railways unless we have a very large expansion in our western provinces. That does not mean that we cannot have expansion in every province of the Dominion, but the conditions and the situation are different in the west, and it is most likely that the expansion will occur in the west in the not distant future.
Railway Freight Rates

The Prime Minister made a trip through the western provinces last year and gave some very glowing accounts as to what the government had done in regard to the Crows-nest pass agreement. I am going to read one or two quotations from speeches he made at that time. Speaking at Winnipeg he said:
Having stated that measures for the advantage of western Canada would also be of advantage to eastern Canada-
I want to call attention to that statement.
Premier King said the administration had restored the Crowsnest pass agreement after a careful inquiry by a committee of the House of Commons, and it was now in force as in the old days of the Liberal administration. "The question of discrimination is now before the railway commission," he said. "It would be improper while the matter is sub judice for me to discuss that question or express an opinion one way or another; but I believe that the system which has been adopted of having railway matters referred to a railway commission independent altogether of parliament, acting as fair-minded, honest and straightforward judges, will be found the most effective and most satisfactory manner of dealing with all questions of importance that arise."
Speaking at Saskatoon on October 7, the Prime Minister said:
When I spoke in Northumberland a few weeks ago, I defined policies and I defined them in the manner I will in western Canada. I intend to say the same thing in western Canada that I told them in eastern Canada. I haven't one message for the west and one for the east. I have one message for all Canada. I told the east that we were carrying out our promises made before election. The Crowsnest agreement was made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and we were carrying out his policies. That was the statement I made in eastern Canada. It is the statement of our position in western Canada.
Again at Edmonton on October 11, the Prime Minister said:
On taking office he had sought to carry out the policies of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and hoped that we would obtain representation in the west that would enable him to follow out those policies to their conclusion. He reminded the gathering that it was under Liberal auspices that the Canadian Northern railway which served Vegreviille had been built, and also that it was an early Liberal administration which had established the Crowsnest pass agreement; and the present administration which had restored it after it had been suspended by the Tories.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I believe the Prime Minister was quite sincere, and I almost think that in his heart to-day he would like to see those promises fulfilled.

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext:
Does the
hon. member realize that the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada rendered some few months ago changes the whole situation with regard to the Crowsnest pass agreement?

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext:
I understand the situation
thoroughly, and I understand the decision that has been given by the Supreme court since the Prime Minister made those state-

ments. But I am perfectly sure that parliament has the same power to-day as it always has had to remove any discrimination, and that in fact it could have removed that discrimination when it took place at the very time the Crowsnest pass agreement came into effect. The idea at that time was to wait until the decision of the railway commission in regard to discrimination was given. We had some dispute with the railway commission. Instead of removing the discrimination, the commission abrogated the Crowsnest pass agreement altogether. I am not blaming the government, but at the same time I know they could have removed the discrimination if they had so desired. I am sure the Prime Minister would like to see those promises fulfilled, and to let us have the Crowsnest pass agreement, or a quid pro quo in western Canada. Conditions have perhaps changed to some extent since 1867, but I want to repeat that the west will not be satisfied unless they have a maximum rate fixed for westbound traffic, just as it has been fixed for eastbound traffic. This is our Magna Charta. We are situated in the centre of the continent, and while hon. gentlemen claim they have tremendous faith in the railway commission, that commission is only human and we do not know what it might do. With respect to other parts of Canada, it would be a serious matter if they had to pay the maximum rates, but in the case of the prairie provinces it would not only be serious, but it would mean bankruptcy to the people of the west. Transportation through the western provinces is of more consequence than it is in any other part of the Dominion of Canada. That is the reason why we feel so strongly on this subject and are so anxious to see that the prairie provinces get a square deal in this matter.
In conclusion, I repeat that I have no thought of hostility towards any part of Canada. I know something about the troubles and difficulties of the Maritime provinces. I am sure we have the warmest feelings towards the people down there and we wish to see them prosperous and happy. The same is true with regard to British Columbia and the far west. We have the warmest feelings towards the people in that part of the country. We want to work hand in hand with every section of this Dominion in order to make it a happy and prosperous country.

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext:
This question is of paramount importance to British Columbia. For nearly twenty years the governments, both Conservative and Liberal, have been fighting for fair treatment in regard to freight rates. The commencement of this contest was dur-

Railway Freight Rates
ing the premiership of Sir Richard McBride. To-day that province faces, perhaps, a more delicate situation than it has ever done in the past. The industrial, commercial, shipping and agricultural future of British Columbia stand in the balance. If the scales of justice and fair play weigh out equitable treatment on this important question, our future is assured and our province will prosper. This legislation is rather late in being brought down. I do not know of any question more important to the people of Canada than that of freight rates. It has been under the consideration of parliament for the last three years or more. Evidence in great detail and from men best qualified to give it has been taken before a special committee; hearings have been had before the Board of Railway Commissioners; reports on previous occasions have been made to the House; legislation has been brought down, and at this juncture, on the eve of an election, the government brings forward a policy which is capable of being interpreted as being calculated to remedy the ills or grievances of every particular section of the country. The order in council is of a very general nature. The legislation, however, is specific on one point, and that point seriously and vitally affects the province from which I come. The legislation states in clear terms that maximum rates on grain and flour moving eastward are fixed according to the Crowsnest pass agreement, but the Crowsnest pass agreement, which was limited formerly to certain areas or districts, is now made applicable to both railway systems, and in order that the government may be more specific in its intention, notice has been given by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. GraJham) that an amendment will be made making it very clear and precise that the advantage o-f comparatively low rates on grain and flour shall not be given to British Columbia.
In my opinion, that is politically an affront to the people of my province. They have carried on the fight for many years. The merits of the case cannot be and never have been denied. It seems to me that the whole point involved in this discussion, so far as British Columbia is concerned, is this: On what principle or basis of reasoning does the government grant a special right and privilege for grain moving eastward to a certain market and deny that same right and privilege for grain moving westward to the same market, the government having spent many millions of dollars on grain elevators and port development in the city of Vancouver? Has the government an answer to that question? I won-277
der if there is even a plausible excuse. I wonder if there is any excuse at all, beyond the plain, patent fact that it is an act of political expediency on the eve of an election in order to gain the support of the middle west provinces. I do not think I am overstating the case in putting it in that way. We, in the activities of the House, are well aware of the suggestions and manoeuvring backward and forwards which for many years have gone on in connection with the Crowsnest pass agreement, the rates of which, so far as they affect British Columbia, were simply iniquitous. No one will deny that. Now, when it is seriously the intention of the government to tackle this great question, one that goes to the root of our economic body, of every activity which we have, industrial, commercial and otherwise, instead of taking hold of it in a statesmanlike manner in the interest of the whole nation and giving to an expert body who understand the problem and the complications of the matter, authority to determine the question from one end to the other, they give the Board of Railway Commissioners authority to determine the question on everything but grain and flour moving eastward. I am not saying that the middle provinces have reason to be displeased with the measure of success which they have obtained. The point which I wish to make and which I would ask the minister to answer now if he can, is this: On what basis of reason, policy or fair play, does he determine a course of legislation which fixes definite maximum rates on grain moving eastward to a certain market 'but denies them on grain moving westward to the same market?

speechtext:
I have answered it at
least four times this afternoon. The fact is that the Crowsnest pass agreement is allowed to remain on the statute book as regards grain and flour. The Crowsnest pass agreement never affected British Columbia, and there is no clause in the bill or in the amendment which has any reference to British Columbia or that will in any way affect the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners adversely to British Columbia.

speechtext: I think the minister's explanation is a very weak one.

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext: That is the hon. member's opinion, of course.

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext:
There are two features
of his explanation. One is that the Crowsnest pass agreement does not affect British Columbia. The Crowsnest pass agreement vitally affects British Columbia, because since the

Railway Freight Rates

agreement was made, we have had the Panama canal opened giving a new outlet for grain leaving this country and a new route for goods to come in from Europe and certain portions of eastern Canada. The minister has entirely forgotten that the whole situation in regard to the shipment of grain from the prairie provinces has been changed. subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext: That is what I said.

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext: They are cancelling eleven other articles of far-reaching effect. Having put the pruning knife on the tree, why not prune it properly and make it look decent and fair? If they are going to change the Crowsnest pass agreement, as they must do in order to cancel the eleven other articles, they might just as well, in order to be consistent and carry the policy of fairplay to the'other portions of the country affected, make a little addition and say that this rate will apply, not only to grain and flour moving eastward, but to grain and flour moving westward. The minister is quibbling on the matter. This does not go to the root of the problem. I repeat that laying down a policy on a matter of such overwhelming importance to the country, definitely fixing the rate on grain moving in one direction to a given market, and specifically and intentionally denying it to grain moving westward to the same market, is not only inconsistent; it is farcical. It is pure political expediency and nothing else in view of an expected election this fall. In making these remarks I do not wish to cast any reflection on the Progressive members to my left. They have felt themselves under an injustice in the matter of freight rates and they have fought for the interests of their section of the country; and the government has been weak enough to yield to this sectional demand without proper regard to other portions of Canada.

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext: I hope the hon. member does not imply that members in this section are not as much interested in securing lower rates on grain and flour to Vancouver as are members from British Columbia.

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext:
Not a bit. I quite understand that hon. members to my left are in accord with us in the view that the rates should extend to westbound grain, inasmuch as the commodity goes to the same markets and is produced by the same people. So far as

British Columbia is concerned, when the order in council appeared it was published in a local newspaper there which had taken a very active and aggressive part in the freight rates question. A report was published spreading right across the paper and a great deal of credit was given to the government on account of the fact, as alleged in the report, that a new era had dawned for Bri:ish Columbia. On that same day, the 6th of June, editorials appeared in both the leading Vancouver newspapers, and for the information of the committee as well as the members of the government I should like to read one or two short extracts from these articles. The Vancouver Province in its leading editorial of that date says:
"Equitable treatment" is the thing British Columbia [DOT] has been fighting for. We have never asked for more. We shall not be content with less. And there is very good reason to believe that with the practically free hand now given the railway commission, we shall achieve our end. Practically since its establishment, the railway commission has devoted itself to the ironing out of unjust discrimination, wherever found, and there are many precedents in its past decisions. The limitation of its powers under the Crowsnest Act brought it to a full stop. Now, it can get under way again.
Further on the editorial has this to say, which I would commend to the attention of the minister:
Two things British Columbia has been seeking in her freight rates fight: an equitable rate on grain, westbound, which will enable us to reach farther into the prairies for cargoes to fill our ships; and an equitable rate on other commodities moving from the Pacific coast eastward which will enable our manufacturers and wholesalers to get a fair share of the prairie business.
In the Morning Sun of June 9, three days afterwards, that newspaper reconsidered its position and editorially advised the government and the Prime Minister in these words:
In their order-in-council requesting the railway board to equalize freight rates, Premier Mackenzie King and his colleagues have shown a vague intent to do the west justice.
That vague intent is not good enough.
The order-in-council decrees that the Crowsnest maximum rate on eastbound grain shall not be exceeded. It would have been just as easy, instead of generalizing on equalization, to have said plainly and definitely that that maximum Crowsnest rate on grain should not be exceeded eastbound or westbound.
Nothing less than such a plain definite statement can actually bring British Columbia into the Canadian confederation.
Nothing less can give the people of British Columbia full Canadian citizenship.
The task of making British Golumbia a Canadian province or an alien province rests with Mackenzie King, not with the Railway Board.
There you have the views of two newspapers, one of no particular political complexion and the other frequently a supporter of the government. But I commend to the government the words of a gentleman welll informed on

Railway Freu/hl Rates
this question and on all its intricacies, an ardent supporter of the present administration, an aggressive, fighting leader of the Liberal party in British Columbia, Premier John Oliver. He has never been known to sympathize with anything that savoured particularly of Conservative policy, nor has he ever been known to support the Conservative cause in any way whatever. Let me read from a signed statement given by Mr. Oliver to the local newspapers, which statement I would urge the government to consider carefully. Mr. Oliver says:
I say, without any reservation, that under the pro. posed legislation the Board of Railway Commissioners may allow any discriminatory rate against the westbound movement of grain and flour, either for export or home consumption, and while I have no desire or intention to in any way reflect upon the honour of the Board of Railway Commissioners, or of any member thereof, yet I have in mind that the majority of the members of the board are the same men who authorized the discriminatory rates under which we have suffered so -long and so grievously.
I do not share Mr. Oliver's view if it reflects upon the Board of Railway Commissioners because I believe that the board is well qualified to handle the matter. He goes on:
Should they in the future authorize a discriminatory rate with the proposed legislation upon the statute book, it would be hopeless to appeal to the Supreme court as a matter of law, and I would have no confidence in appealing to a government which, in the face of the protests that have been made, would persist in placing legislation, as proposed, on the statute books.
This is a Liberal premier in British Columbia advising his Liberal friends in Ottawa. Mr. Oliver continues:

Mr. Chairman, the question of freight rates is one of the most important before this House and the country, especially in view of the fact that the government owns the greater part of the railway mileage of the country, and when the Canadian National Railway system does not earn sufficient to pay its bills the people are called upon to meet the deficit. I think it is well that we should know what part of the country's business is paying its way, whether that in the east, the west or the centre; and, furthermore, what part of the country is paying the greater proportion of the taxes. Consequently I shall take up some little time to explain my views.
The Crowsnest pass agreement, which we have heard so much about, was entered into in 1897 between the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on the one side and the government of Canada representing the people on the other side. Under that agreement it was provided that the rates-now known as the Crowsnest pass rates-should not exceed certain maxima. I presume it never entered into the minds of the parties to the agreement that conditions would ever change. At that time wages, materials, and other costs that enter into the operation of railways were very different to what they are to-day. That arrangement continued for many years, and the Canadian Pacific Railway and other roads kept their rates much below the maxima fixed thereunder. Ultimately during the war railway operating costs went so high that the Crowsnest pass agreement had to be suspended for a period of years. At the expiration of that period there was a clamour, especially from the west, for a reversion to the Crowsnest pass rates. Unfortunately the cost of railway operation at that time did not
9 p.m. justify the restoration of these rates. In 1922 this House appointed a committee to investigate the freight rate question, and that committee summoned before it not only all the railway magnates 
of Canada but also many from across the border. Mr. Beatty, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, usually acted as spokesman for the railways. He made several propositions, the final one being for a general reduction of 20 per cent in the rates on all basic commodities to all parts of Canada. That committee finally, by a small majority, passed a resolution recommending the acceptance of this proposition. But the western members rebelled and said they must have the Crowsnest pass rates regardless of what any other part of Canada might get. Naturally they might be expected to take this course, but I did not quite agree with the government's yielding to the demand The outcome has been that whilst, the prairie provinces have secured the restoration of the Crowsnest pass rates, which represent approximately a 35 per cent reduction in the freight rates on grain to the head of the lakes, the rest of Canada got a reduction of only 6 per cent in - the rates on basic commodities.

When the McAdoo arrangement which had been formulated and all worked out in Indianapolis, or somewhere else across the line, was proposed to Canada, the Canadian railways were simply advised that on such and such a date this schedule of wages and classification of labour would come into force. The railways of Canada at that time held a conference, at which the question was discussed from all angles, and they finally decided that, whether or not it was possible for the United States to accept this remuneration and classification of labour, so far as Canada was concerned it was absolutely impossible, and they notified the Canadian government that they would not accept the award. The government, of which my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition was a member, then passed an order in council ordering the Canadian railways to accept that schedule of wages and classification of labour. I wonder if it has ever entered the minds of the people of Canada that that action has placed the railways of Canada in practically an impossible position to give us the rates we should have? It tied them up to a remuneration and classification of labour that the present conditions of this country do not justify, and meant an increase in railway rates.
As I have said before in this House, there are three parties to this business: There is the producer. Whether he be a farmer, a lumberman, a miner, or whatever his calling may be, if he is producing goods, he is a producer. Then there are the transportation companies. No matter whether they operate by land or sea, the people who are engaged in carrying the products of this country from the sources of production to the sources of consumption are engaged in transportation. The third element is the distributor. It does not matter whether he is a wholesaler, a jobber or a peddler; he is selling goods, and therefore is a distributor. We have, then, these three classes, and if one of these classes gets more than their fair share, the other classes get less than their share. That is the situation in connection with the railways. The railway employees are getting more money than the business of the country can stand, and that has been brought about to a large extent by the railways, against their will and desire, being forced to accept a schedule of remuneration that was not possible for this country to pay. Whilst this schedule of wages might possibly be worked out in the United States, we must bear in mind that the
United States have a population of 437 for each mile of railway, whereas we have just a fraction over 200 people for each mile of railway. That means the United States railways have, or should have, double the passenger and freight traffic for each mile of railway that we have, and consequently they can stand a scale of wages and a classification of labour that we in Canada cannot stand. That is the reason, to my mind, why the government of this country should say to international labour, whether it is railway labour or any other kind:	We would be glad if
you would stay at home, run your business as you like, and we will attend to our business; we have no objection to our citizens organizing, if they wish, to carry on their work, but we absolutely refuse to allow international labour and international labour organizations across the border to come here and dictate terms to us; we are supplying the money; we are running this railway; we are running the whole country, and we propose to run our business in accordance with our ability to pay, and meet the conditions as we find them in Canada; we are not in a position to meet the conditions that exist across the line, especially in railway matters, where you have more than double the population per mile of railway that we have. I do not think, Mr. Chairman, I will talk much longer on that score. My system does not allow of talking too much.

speechtext:
I do not
know whether my hon. friend is a student of railway freight rates or not, but many questions enter into this matter of freight rate decisions as regards British Columbia. The question is not merely one of grain going ' west. There are the commodity rates which people in British Columbia enjoy on east-bound traffic. All these problems are committed to the railway commission which he and his friends say is the proper body to deal with them. I am coming to that point in a moment. To follow up the suggestion of the hon. member for Brandon, no matter how extreme our views may be having regard to particular localities, we must realize that, in the last analysis, there must be some body composed of experts to deal with the matter of rate-fixing and all the problems connected therewith if results are to be obtained. How could a committee of this House, for instance, discuss the rate structure of this country and find out what would be equitable? Hence it is that, once this question of grain and flour was dealt with, the government proposed, and we propose now by our order in council, to submit to the railway commission the matter of dealing with rate-fixing in a most equitable way having regard to the situation throughout the country. The order in council states:
The committee therefore advise that the board be directed to make a thorough investigation of the rate structures of railways and railway companies subject to the jurisdiction of parliament with a view to the eslablishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure, which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities, so as to permit of the freest possible interchange of commodities between the various provinces and territories of the Dominion and the expansion of its trade, both foreign and domestic, having due regard to the needs of its agricultural and other basic industries, and in particular to:
(a)	The claim, asserted on behalf of the Maritime provinces that they are entitled to the restoration of the Tate basis which they enjoyed prior to 1919;
(b)	The encouragement of the movement of traffic through Canadian ports;
(c)	The increased traffic westward and eastward through Pacific coast ports owing to the expansion of trade with the Orient and to the transportation of products through the Panama canal.
What we have done, referring to our British Columbia friends, is this. We have asked the railway commission to approach the solution of this question on the broadest possible basis in order to attain the purposes which are set out in this order in council. We ask them particularly to take into consideration the traffic eastward and westward through Pacific coast ports owing to the expansion of trade in that part of Canada. Among the changed conditions that have taken place in this country has been the wonderful development of trade in British Columbia as a result of the opening of the Panama canal. It has been a marvellous change which has slipped into the business life of this country quietly, and yet it has created conditions of the greatest possible advantage and holding out the certainty of development in western Canada through that part which is contiguous to the Pacific coast by reason of this new method of water transportation that has been developed. There is also the trade with the Orient and the great consumption of grain and other products that has developed in Japan and China. All these constitute a new business situation that did not exist in 1897, that hardly existed ten years ago.; This is a development of the last four or five years. These are special matters which are submitted to the railway commission and which they must have regard to when they come to deal with the question of the equalization of rates.
There is also the situation that has existed in the Maritime provinces and to which my hon. colleague has referred this afternoon. That is a situation which is hardly appreciated by this House. From 1877 down to 1919, for a period of forty-two years, what was known as the Intercolonial railway with various extensions constituted the only publicly-owned and operated railway in Canada, with the exception of the addition which was made later on when the Transcontinental was built to Winnipeg. But the operation of the Intercolonial was carried on under terms and conditions which caused the people of the Maritime provinces to rely upon the federal government to see to it that their interests were properly protected. In the British North America Act the construction of that railway is specially provided for, and no public work is provided for in that act other than that railway. In the pre-confederation conferences which ied up to the formation of the Dominion the construction of that railway was recognized as an absolute condition upon the Maritime provinces gtoing into confederation. There

Railway Freight Rates

would have been no Canada at all had it not been for the assurance given in that respect. And after that railway was constructed it was operated for a period of forty-two years by the federal government in accordance with what the people in that part of Canada understood to be the confederation agreement. It was operated not primarily with a view to making money, although the railway paid its way all through that period; some years there was a substantial surplus while in other years there was a small deficit. As a result of that method of operation of the Intercolonial railway we were able to obtain access to central Canada with a great many of our natural products; and, mark you, the manufacturers of central Canada were able to come down into our markets by virtue of the conditions under which the railway was operated. Under these circumstances there was an enormous exchange of products between the two sections of the Dominion, and as a matter of fact the Maritime provinces are still a great factor in the business of the manufacturers of central Canada. Hon. gentlemen speak about certain rates having existed under the Crowsnest agreement from 1897 to 1919, a period of twenty-two years. Well, this charter of our existence as part of the Dominion of Canada has been m existence almost twice as long, for some forty-two years. Now the government asks the railway commission, when it comes to deal with the whole question of freight rates, to consider the claim made by our people in the Maritime provinces to the right to have maintained the rate basis which they enjoyed prior to 1919.

The Minister of Railways in presenting this bill has stated that there are three courses open to parliament. And there is a third or middle .course suggested, such as that taken here. On that .point I emphatically disagree with" the minister, and I think I can Show him that he is in error in submitting that view to the House. In. my opinion the Crowsnest agreement is in full force and effect to-day; but its force and effect is limited to those points which were on the Canadian Faoific Railway in 1897. As the minister has said, the agreement is an impossibility. It is an impossibility if the view he presents is correct, and it is equally an impossibility if my own view is accepted. We are agreed that the Crowsnest agreement is impossible in its present form; but I disagree emphatically with the minister when he states that the railway board would be bound, if the agreement were left as it is now, to give similar rates throughout the country and that Ithe effect would be to wreck the railway companies. If the minister had read the decision of the Supreme court, and if the Minister of National Defence (Mir. Macdonald, Pictou) had read it, they would not have made the statements which they made this afternoon and evening in regard to this agreement. Let me read from the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada as it appears in the printed pamphlet distributed to us. It states quite clearly that the points affected by the agreement are only those that were on the railway at- the time the agreement came into force.

Therefore I say the board would not be bound to give similar rates throughout Canada, for this decision goes on to say:
When such maxima are fixed by special acts, they must be regarded as exceptions intentionally made by parliament from the application of its general policy against discrimination. .	. . Discrimination so authorized by parliament itself cannot be regarded as unjust or prohibitive.
In the face of that decision, how can the minister state to this House and the country that the railway commission would be bound to give similar rates to those authorized by the agreement on similar commodities throughout the country? As a matter of fact, the Crowsnest pass agreement under the decision of' the Supreme Court of Canada is dead, and should be buried. Why attempt to revive a dead horse? My hon. friends from the west may think that we in British Columbia have very different views on the subject of freight rates to those entertained by them. Not at all. In fact I think that members in this end of the House are in agreement on the point that the basic commodities of this country, more particularly wheat and flour, are entitled to very special . consideration, because obviously the west is an inland empire and must be given an. . outlet at reasonable freight rates (for its principal products. But there are different ways of doing it. In view of public opinion not only in the west but throughout Canada,
I think the railway board would have great difficulty in refusing to authorize rates that are distinctly favourable on wheat and flour.
I further think that the railway board would adjust the matter so that full justice would be done not only to Manitoba and the eastern portion of Saskatchewan, but also to the western portion of Saskatchewan and the whole of Alberta and British Columbia. There would not be any discrimination between grain flowing eastward and grain flowing westward. There would not be the discrimination which this government has seen fit to introduce between the ports of Vancouver and Buffalo and New York. For that is one of the effects of this proposed legislation. Buffalo and New York will reap the harvest flowing from the western provinces by reason of these favoured rates whereas Alberta and the western portion of Saskatchewan will be asked to pay nearly double these rates to get their grain out by Vancouver. That is the sort of discrimination which this government is guilty of in sponsoring this bill.
There is a second very important feature in this measure. Again I take issue with the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mac-

Since the railway board was created British Columbia and Alberta have always had the right to come before it and present a case based on unjust discrimination caused by rates on grain and flour under the Crowsnest pass agreement. A fair comparison would be between the two ocean ports of Vancouver and St. John, and I am able to give the figures in that regard. From Vancouver to St. John the rate is 103i cents, the same as from Vancouver to Plaster Rock, while from St. John to Vancouver the rate is 142 per hundred. And they are both ocean ports. I think a worse comparison may be given. Our British Columbia friends have always contended that the mountain rate militates against that province, but I think I can show by comparison that it must be an advantage to British Columbia to ship over the mountains because they can ship from Vancouver over the mountains to Plaster Rock, New Brunswick, at 103i whereas to ship from Plaster Rock to Calgary or Edmonton -and this does not go over the mountains-we are obliged to pay 126, or 22j cents per hundred pounds more from our point in New Brunswick to Calgary or Edmonton than the lumber man pays from Vancouver to Plaster Rock. To my mind this is discrimination of the worst kind. I took this matter up with the railway commission some time ago and I shall quote some of the correspondence that passed on the subject. I may say, by the way, that the rates I have given were confirmed by the railway commission. I had obtained these rates but thinking that possibly they were not correct I went to the commission to have them verified and accompanying the statement of rates there was a memorandum setting forth some of the reasons. The memorandum stated:
.So far, therefore, as the comparison of rates proving anomalies or disparities eastbound versus westbound is concerned, in my opinion, it is meaningless, because the movements are not comparable, and, further, if there was any actual movement westbound from some of these shipping points shown, unquestionably the rates would be on a different basis as it is evident the rates shown in the statement are largely ''paper rates."
I shall quote a paragraph from my letter in reply to that statement, which I regarded as a most remarkable one. In another place the statement had been made that the only movement of lumber west was hardwood flooring. In reply to this I said:
"With regard to his statement that the westbound movement of lumber is confined largely to hardwood flooring, I think possibly this is correct, as it is possibly the only lumber we have in eastern Canada that would sell dear enough in the western market to stand the present very high freight rate.
With regard to his other statement, that if there was any actual movement westbound from some of these shipping points shown, unquestionably the rates would be on a different basis. I think in this latter instance he has stated the case backwards. If he had said, if the rates were on a different basis, unquestionably
there would have been a movement westbound from some of these shipping points, he would undoubtedly have been right as I have no doubt that there is a good market in the middle western provinces for the spruce lumber of New Brunswick for building purposes, and I hope to take up with your board at your earliest convenience the question of securing a cheaper rate on our lumber from the Maritime province ports to central and western Canada.
To that Mir. Commissioner Boyce replied:
Speaking for myself, and in accord with the replies that the board has given to similar requests for reductions or equalizations of specific rates, it would appear that until the whole rate structure is dealt with on a definite policy, probably to be decided by the government, it would, I think, be undesirable for the board to deal with specific applications until it has before it the general policy.
That is ithe policy, Mr. Chairman, which I presume we are now considering. I am not at all satisfied with the policy 'brought down by the government, because, as I said before, in endeavouring to iron out the discriminations that obtain under the Crowsnest pass agreement since the decision by the Supreme court, they propose to take away all the advantages the east ever enjoyed under that agreement, and to cut out the discrimination on grain and flour coming east iby extending the operation of this commodity rate to a very large degree indeed, i think the Minister of Railways said that the old act applied to something less than three thousand miles of railway in the west.

export the ralte is only 49i cents per hundred pounds. So for domestic purposes we have to pay 20 cents .per hundred pounds more. This is the sort of discrimination we suffer in Neiw Brunswick.
iNow, with regard to the increases in the rates on local oommodities, I was hardly able to follow my hon. friend from Kings, P.EJ. (Mr. Hughes) to-night, although I am usually able to agree with (him, especially on tariff matters, He argued that a lowering of freight rates even between the Maritime provinces and central Canada would not be a benefit to the Maritime [provinces.

speechtext: We do have commodities that we want to ship to the western provinces. For instance, last winter because of a shortage *there we shipped potatoes to Calgary.

speechtext: Last year potatoes were bringing a price in the Maritime provinces far below what it cost to produce them. That was an exceptional condition.

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext: We did get a special concession to Winnipeg and points west, but we couM not get lany similar concession to other points nearer at hand1. We shipped potatoes as far west as Calgary and North Batbleford. I traced three of the shipments through, and I found that potatoes for which our farmers got 22 cents a bushel retailed in North Battleford at $1.85 a bushel. If that market is any good to the fanners of the Maritime provinces, they would need a magnifying igflass to detect it, because the cost of producing those potatoes was at least 40 cents a bushel.
