speechtext: What was the rate to Edmonton?

subtopic: BILL TO AMEND THE RAILWAY ACT, '1919
speechtext:
I do not recall at the moment. We got two reductions last winter in order to get our potatoes there at all, rather than dump them over the bank. I find that the rate from Andover to Montreal, a distance of 505 miles, was 17 cents per hundred pounds in 1913; in 1919 it was 19 cents per hundred pounds; but to-day it is 324 cents per hundred pounds, or an increase of nearly 100 per cent over 1913. This is a prohibitive rate for such a short haul. This is what is affecting us very severely in the Maritime provinces, and we want some relief if it is at all possible to get it. As I said, I am afraid the pious wish contained in the order in council will not get us very far. I do not think that the members of this House are qualified to set specific rates in any direction, but I do think this parliament

must lay down a policy under which the railway commission will fix the rates. In this proposed legislation there is no policy for Canada as a whole. There is a special provision for a certain section of the Dominion on a specific commodity, and the rest of us will have to take pot luck. I think the railway commission is the logical body to set rates. At the same time, I have not always been satisfied with the rates they have set, due largely, I think, to the fact that they have been interfered with by special legislation, but more often by special pressure brought to bear by different interests in this country. I think the railway commission should be put in just the same position as *the Canadian National Railways-it should be absolutely free from political interference in the fixing of rates. I do not think there should even be a pious wish sent to the commission from the government as to what it should do. If the commission do not make just and equitable rates, I think the government should fire the commissioners so fast that we would forget their names. That is what should happen to them if they do not deal out justice to all parts of Canada.
Another matter was drawn to my attention by the lumber company that wrote me about their special rates. This is possibly the second largest lumber company in eastern Canada, and in addition to their lumbering operations they own and operate a number of large farms where they have embarked on the breeding of pure-bred stock to a considerable extent. During the past winter they sent their stock man to Ontario to purchase some pure-bred cattle. He bought two carloads, and they were loaded at a place called Inker-man, about ninety miles west of Montreal. By the way, in writing me about the freight rates on lumber the company incidentally mentioned this shipment of cattle, and said they were not able to get the same rate on them as would have been accorded them on a western shipment. I am interested in the raising of pure-bred cattle myself, and I wrote them for further particulars. Their letter in reply is dated May 23, 1925:
Your letter of the 16th instant referring to rates on cattle.
The particulars in regard to this are, that this year, we bought two carloads of pure-bred cattle in Ontario, some ninety miles west of Montreal, and loaded them at Inkerman station, Ontario. Mr. Irvine, Canadian Pacific Railway station agent there, notified our men that there was a cheaper rate on pure-bred cattle, but it onlly applied to cattle being shipped west and net coming east of Montreal.

agreement might have had a sympathetic effect on the rate on cattle. I thought there must be something wrong, and I took this matter up with the Live Stock department, and I received a letter from the Live Stock Commissioner, dated June 15th, reading as follows:
Following conversation this morning and with reference to letter, herewith returned, addressed to you by the Fraser Lumber Company, I beg to advise that, in shipping a carload of pure-bred cattle as between points in eastern Canada, the shipper cannot do better than ship at the ordinary carload rate.
It is only in cases of less than carloads that the reduced pure-bred rate applies. Furthermore, even in shipping less than carloads of pure-bred live stock, when there are more than say five cattle in the car, it usually works out better even in this case to ship at the carload rate than to ship at the pure-bred rate, which is based on a considerably higher tariff.
The reduced rates in connection with the shipment of carlogds of pure-bred live stock, apply only in connection with shipments as between points east and points west. In cases of this kind, the settlers' effects rate applies, which is about 30 per cent less than the ordinary rate.
As I said, in delving into this matter I have not been able to find a case with regard to railway rates -where the Maritime provinces seem to be getting an even 'break with anybody. We seem to be getting it where the chicken got the axe in almost every case.
With regard to rates between the Maritime provinces and other parts of Canada, I do not agree, however, with the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes) that we have not got any reduction in local rates, especially in New Brunswick.

Yes that is where our
movement went that year. After putting up our case, the representatives of the railroad companies bold us it would be impossible to give us any reduction in rates, and most of those at the meeting were very disappointed. However, I realized that we had taken the matter up wrong. We had had the railway companies send us their traffic men, whose duty it is to go and meet the public, and endeavour to make them believe they are getting a little better deal than anybody else in Canada. I suggested that we should get a small committee to go to Montreal and meet the management of the railroad companies. We did this, and got a reduction of 6 cents per hundred pounds on a rate of 23$ cents, which was a little better than 25 per cent reduction on our potatoes for export, and this did assist materially in the export of our potatoes that year. But this past winter England put an embargo on potatoes, a thing that made me feel as un-British for a few days as anything that has ever happened since I have been a man, especially in view of the preference that we give to British goods coming -to Canada, and by the way, I am still in favour of the British preference. Our only outlet then was Cuba. It was not a very paying market. Potatoes were selling very high in the Canadian west, where they were very scarce, and we therefore set about to get a reduction in the rate to that point, which we accomplished. However, the distance is so great that we were simply able to get the potatoes out there, rather than throwing them out in the spring; we did not make anything on them. [DOT]
That brings me to another point. Our friends speak of the home market. There was a wonderful home market in the Canadian west for Canadian potatoes, but while the consumer there would have to pay this last

winter $1.85 a bushel for our potatoes, we were only able to get 20 cents per bushel for them in New Brunswick. A home market of that kind is not of much benefit to producers in Canada.

If I might digress just at this point, business is being held up in this country by combines in trade, one of which we unearthed in New Brunswick this winter, with the assistance of the Combines Investigation Act. I know my right hon. friend to my right (Mr. Meighen) has sneered at that act more than once, but I hope he will read the interim report of the investigation that has been carried on in New Brunswick during the past winter. I think it will help him to realize that, after all, that act is a pretty good act, and that it is needful we should go after some of these people.

speechtext:
Our western friends
have told us that their rates are higher than in eastern Canada, but they were very careful not to compare them with the rates in the United States for corresponding distances to the head .of the lakes. On looking over this list-I will make only one comparison-I see that from Edmonton, Alberta, to Fort William, a distance of 1.267 miles, the rate on wheat is 36 cents per one hundred pounds, while from Stonehill, Montana, to Duluth, Minnesota, a distance of 1,265 miles, the rate is 52i cents per one hundred pounds.
In our case in the east we have no advantage over our American cousins in freight rates. We are a little nearer the seaboard than our American cousins in the state of Maine, but we have to quote, when we ship to Cuba, from 15 to 20 cents a bag under our American cousins' price, in order to get into that market at all, and we have to pay our own freight rates, which are heavy enough. We have also

been subject to the "middle against both ends" in the potato trade in New Brunswick, but I hope we shall be able to eliminate that if we follow up the report of this investigation and punish the guilty as they should be punished.
I do not wish at this late hour to take up any more time, but I thought in view of the fact that I was not able to support the Crowsnest pass legislation this year, and having regard to the fact that I did support it in 1922, I felt in justice to myself I should give my reasons. I hope I have made it clear both to the House and the country why I have changed my mind on this matter. If the Crowsnes't pass agreement applied, as I believed it applied in 1922, I would support it to-day; but I cannot approve of the government's legislation which deprives the east of any benefit it ever had under the Crowsnest pass agreement and extends it more fully to freight coming east.
